key_terms.meaning: Step-up transformer with a thick few-turn primary and a thin many-turn secondary wound on one iron core
Low-voltage path: battery → ignition switch → coil primary → switching device → earth
High-voltage path from the coil secondary winding to the plug(s) and back to earth
n = N₂/N₁, the secondary turns divided by the primary turns; it sets the voltage step-up
Time, or cam angle, for which primary current is allowed to build before it is interrupted
Crank angle before top dead centre at which the plug is fired, written as °BTDC
Voltage at which the plug gap ionises and a spark current starts to flow
Distance between the centre and earth electrode of a plug, typically 0.7–1.1 mm
Number saying how quickly a plug tip sheds heat to the cylinder head; low number = hot plug
Power transistor that switches the coil primary current on the ECU's command
Timing and dwell read from maps of speed, load and coolant temperature held in the ECU memory
One coil fires two plugs together; the plug on the exhaust stroke sparks for no useful effect
A separate coil mounted directly on each plug, so high-tension leads disappear
Light output divided by electrical input power, in lumens per watt (lm/W)
Iodine or bromine returns evaporated tungsten to the filament, so the bulb runs hotter and lasts longer
Metal-halide arc lamp struck and run by a high-voltage ballast unit
Semiconductor junction that emits light; needs a constant-current driver, not a fixed voltage
Shape of the light patch on the road, with a sharp upper edge that limits glare to oncoming traffic
Small motor that tilts the headlamp so the cut-off stays level when the car is loaded
Key holding a passive chip that answers a coded radio challenge from the immobiliser

takeaways: A coil ignition system makes high voltage only because the primary current is cut quickly, so the collapsing field links the many secondary turns.
The voltage a plug needs rises with gap size and with compression pressure, so a worn plug or a lean, hot engine misfires first at high load.
Electronic ignition replaces the contact breaker with a transistor, and the ECU then owns dwell and timing as mapped values.
Distributorless and direct ignition push the coil to the plug, removing rotor, cap and long high-tension leads with their losses.
Compare lamps by efficacy in lm/W and by colour, then by life and cost over the whole vehicle life.
Each lighting group has its own beam pattern, colour, switching circuit and legal limit, not just its own bulb.
Adaptive lighting is a closed loop: sensors measure steering angle and vehicle pitch, and a motor moves the beam.
The cluster and the immobiliser are bus nodes, so diagnosis means looking at frames and codes, not only at wires.
bank_note: Long answers here are 'explain with a labelled sketch, then compare' — coil versus electronic versus direct ignition, and halogen versus HID versus LED lighting — so carry a diagram and a comparison table into the hall.

bank.q: Draw a labelled diagram of a coil ignition system and explain step by step how interrupting the primary current produces a spark at the plug.
outline: Primary path: battery, switch, ballast, primary winding, contact breaker, earth
Current builds to about 4–5 A; energy stored in the magnetic field
Points open: current falls quickly, field collapses, flux cuts the secondary turns
Turns ratio and rate of collapse give several thousand volts, raised to 10–20 kV or more
Capacitor across the points suppresses arcing and speeds up the collapse
High voltage goes through rotor and cap to the correct plug, jumps the gap to earth

bank.q: What decides the voltage needed to fire a spark plug? Explain the effect of electrode gap and compression pressure.
outline: Breakdown needs a field strong enough to ionise the gap; define breakdown voltage
Gap size: larger gap needs more voltage, roughly in proportion
Compression pressure: denser charge needs more volts per millimetre
Electrode temperature and shape affect it; hot tips need less
Plug heat range and fouling change the demand
Why misfire appears first at high load and wide gap

bank.q: Explain how an electronic ignition system uses a sensor and a switching transistor in place of contact breaker points.
outline: Position sensor types: inductive, Hall effect, optical
Signal shape and how the ECU derives crank angle and speed
Igniter power transistor switches the coil current
Dwell computed, so it stays correct with speed and battery voltage
No rubbing parts, no point bounce, longer life, higher current possible
Closed-loop additions: knock sensor retards timing

bank.q: Compare distributorless ignition and direct ignition, and state the advantages of each over a distributor system.
outline: Wasted-spark: one coil per pair, both plugs fire, one spark wasted
Direct: one coil per plug, fired only on compression
No rotor, cap or long HT leads; lower losses and less radio interference
Better timing accuracy, no cap tracking or moisture faults
Easier to combine with knock control per cylinder
Service and cost differences

bank.q: Define luminous efficacy and compare halogen, HID and LED light sources for automotive use.
outline: Efficacy = lumens out ÷ watts in, in lm/W
Halogen: about 20–25 lm/W, warm white, cheap, hot
HID: much higher, needs ballast and strike voltage, blue-white
LED: highest of the three, instant, long life, needs current driver and heat sinking
Also compare life, warm-up, dimming and cost

bank.q: Describe the front and rear lighting groups of a car, giving the beam pattern, colour and switching arrangement of each lamp.
outline: Front: headlamp main and dip with cut-off and asymmetric kick-up, position lamp, indicator, fog lamp
Rear: tail, stop, reversing, indicator, rear fog, registration lamp
Colour rules: white or yellow at front, red at rear, amber for indicators
Switching: stalk, relays and ECU-controlled outputs; brake pedal switch; flasher unit
Legal limits on glare, minimum and maximum intensity

bank.q: A four-cylinder four-stroke engine runs at 3000 rpm with a dwell angle of 52°. Calculate the dwell time in milliseconds and state why dwell must be limited at high speed.
outline: Time for one revolution at 3000 rpm = 60/3000 = 20 ms
Time for one ignition event = 20/2 = 10 ms per distributor revolution basis
Dwell time = (52/360) × 20 ms ≈ 2.9 ms
State that current needs 3–5 ms to reach full value
At high speed the available time falls, so dwell angle is increased by the ECU
Too much dwell overheats the coil

bank.q: A car uses two 55 W halogen headlamps. An LED replacement draws 20 W each for the same light output. For two hours of night driving a day, find the energy saved per year and the money saved at ₹8 per kWh.
outline: Power saved per lamp = 55 − 20 = 35 W; two lamps = 70 W
Energy per day = 70 W × 2 h = 140 Wh = 0.14 kWh
Per year = 0.14 × 365 ≈ 51 kWh
Cost saved = 51 × 8 ≈ ₹410 per year
Add comment on alternator load and fuel saving, plus lamp life

bank.q: Explain, with a sketch, how an automatic headlamp levelling system reacts when a heavy load is placed in the boot.
outline: Ride height sensors on front and rear axle
ECU computes pitch angle from the two signals
Stepper or DC motor drives the headlamp reflector down
Closed loop until the cut-off returns to the set angle
Failsafe: lamps return to a default low position
Why it matters: glare to oncoming traffic

bank.q: Describe the challenge-and-response handshake between a transponder key and an immobiliser, and state what the vehicle does when the answer is wrong.
outline: Coil around the ignition barrel powers the passive chip by induction
ECU sends a challenge; key computes a response from its secret code
Match on the stored code releases the ECU; fuel and spark enabled
Mismatch stores a fault code, keeps the engine cranking but not firing, and may flash a telltale
Coding of new keys, and why the secret is not sent over the air

bank.q: A wiper system must sweep, park and offer two speeds plus intermittent wiping. Explain the circuit and the role of each part.
outline: Permanent-magnet DC motor with three brushes for two speeds
Worm gearbox reduces speed and increases torque
Park switch keeps the motor supplied until the park position is reached
Intermittent operation by a timer or ECU pulse relay
Washer pump motor and non-return valve
Rain sensor variant and load-sensing stall protection

bank.q: Analyse why ignition timing must be advanced as engine speed rises and retarded as load rises, and how knock limits the advance.
outline: Flame takes a fixed time to burn; at higher speed it must start earlier
At high load the charge is denser and burns faster, so less advance is needed
Too much advance: peak pressure too early, negative work, knock
Knock sensor detects the characteristic vibration; ECU retards in steps and creeps back
Trade-off between efficiency, emissions and protection
Effect on exhaust temperature and catalyst

bank.q: Evaluate the case for fitting LED headlamps instead of halogen lamps on a low-cost Indian car, covering efficacy, cost, heat, legality and service life.
outline: Efficacy and current draw, and the effect on alternator and fuel
Purchase price against life and replacement labour
Heat path: halogen radiates heat forward, LED must conduct it back to a heatsink
Beam pattern and cut-off: a lamp designed for a reflector must match the housing, else glare
Legality: type approval, colour, aim, self-levelling and washing where required
Driver and oncoming-traffic safety, and the resale and warranty angle

bank.q: Analyse how a modern instrument cluster works as a node on the CAN bus, and what happens when a frame stops arriving.
outline: Cluster is a microcontroller with a CAN transceiver and a display or stepper needles
Frames from engine, ABS and body ECUs carry speed, rpm, temperature, warnings
Identifiers, data length and update rate; missing frames time out
Default and limp behaviour: needles to zero, telltales on, stored fault codes
Diagnosis through the diagnostic connector rather than probing wires
Contrast with the older directly wired cluster

bank.q: Evaluate adaptive front lighting: what it gains the driver, what it costs, and where it can fail.
outline: Swivelling beam with steering angle and speed; town, country and motorway modes
Cornering and static cornering lamps
Level sensors and motor keep the cut-off correct under load and braking
Gains: better see-ahead on bends, less glare, higher speed at night
Costs: motors, sensors, ECU, calibration, diagnosis
Failure modes: stuck motor, sensor drift, glare after a bump; failsafe and legal checks

glossary.def: Key-operated multi-position switch that connects battery, ignition, starter and accessory circuits.
Resistor in series with the coil primary that limits current when running and is bypassed during cranking.
Cam-driven mechanical switch in older systems that interrupts the primary current.
Capacitor across the contact breaker that absorbs arcing and speeds up the collapse of the primary current.
Rotating switch that sends the coil's high voltage to each plug in firing order.
Rotating contact inside the distributor cap that bridges the coil lead to one plug terminal at a time.
Speed-dependent weights and springs that rotate the contact plate to advance timing with engine speed.
Diaphragm unit driven by inlet manifold depression that adds advance at light load.
Piezoelectric sensor on the block that detects detonation vibration so the ECU can retard timing.
Plug with a built-in resistor that suppresses radio-frequency interference from the spark.
Lamp using a small arc or LED source, a reflector and a lens to form a sharp cut-off beam.
Low, wide-beam lamp used in poor visibility; rear fog lamps must be red and are limited in intensity.
Symbol lamp in the cluster that reports a system state or fault to the driver.
Motor that moves in fixed angular steps, used for needles and for headlamp levelling.
Two-wire differential serial bus on which ECUs exchange short frames with identifiers and data bytes.
Stored code that names a fault the ECU has detected, read through the diagnostic connector.
System that prevents engine start unless the correct coded key is present.
Optical sensor on the windscreen that detects water and switches the wipers automatically.
Rest position of the wiper blade at the bottom of the screen, held by a switch inside the motor gearbox.
Optical unit that projects speed and warnings onto the windscreen in the driver's line of sight.
Manual or automatic adjustment of headlamp aim to compensate for vehicle load.
Unit of luminous flux, the total light output of a source.
Spark delivered to a cylinder on its exhaust stroke by a coil shared with its pair.
